headline: Two guards passed attacks they had already detected: `b.gateContract.composeGates` reported `serve` after a member gate sanitized, and `b.guardOauth` skipped its redirect_uri and code-replay checks whenever the operator had not supplied a companion object
summary:
Both are the same shape — a control that runs, reaches a verdict, and then loses it — and both are fixed.

Composing gates is the documented way to chain guards, and it discarded what the members found. A single `b.guardCsv` gate answers a spreadsheet-formula payload with `action: "sanitize"`, one critical finding, and the scrubbed bytes. Wrapping that same gate in `composeGates` answered `serve`, no findings, and no scrubbed output — so a caller that trusted the verdict forwarded the original payload and recorded nothing.

`b.guardOauth` skipped two checks silently. Under any compliance posture, an otherwise-valid callback carrying an attacker-controlled `redirect_uri` and a replayed authorization code came back clean, because both checks were conditional on an operator-supplied companion the guard never asked for.

items.title: `composeGates` reported `serve` after a member gate sanitized
items.body:
The composition ran every member correctly and then returned a fixed `serve` decision, dropping three things the caller needs: that a member sanitized at all, the findings that justified it, and the sanitized bytes themselves.

The practical effect is worse than a missing label. A caller told `serve` with no sanitized output has nothing to forward but the original, so the mitigation a member had already applied was thrown away — a CSV cell beginning with `=`, which the recipient's spreadsheet would execute, passed through a chain whose own member had flagged it critical and rewritten it.

A composed gate now reports `sanitize` when any member sanitized, returns the scrubbed bytes, and carries every member's findings. A refusal now carries the findings gathered before it too, so the reason a chain refused is the whole chain's evidence rather than the last gate's half of it.

items.title: `b.guardOauth` skipped code-replay detection when no store was configured
items.body:
`codeReusePolicy` is `"reject"` at every profile, and the module described the check as unconditional and fail-closed. It was neither. The replay lookup — and the fail-closed handling around it — sat inside a branch that only ran when `opts.seenCodeStore` existed, so a store that ERRORED refused the flow while a store that was simply ABSENT let it through with no finding at all.

A missing store answers the same question as a broken one: whether this authorization code has already been exchanged is unknown, and an unknown answer is a denial (RFC 6749 §10.5). Both cases now refuse with `oauth.code-reuse-unverifiable`. Operators who do not want replay protection set `codeReusePolicy: "allow"`, which is unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardOauth` said nothing when `require-exact-allowlist` had no allowlist
items.body:
The strict and balanced profiles set `redirectUriPolicy: "require-exact-allowlist"`, and every compliance posture selects strict. With no `allowedRedirectUris` configured, the exact-match check was skipped entirely — the redirect_uri class the policy exists for, where an attacker-nominated callback carries the authorization code away.

The skip was intentional and the reasoning was written down: the warning was said to belong in the operator's startup audit rather than in per-request findings. No such warning was ever emitted anywhere in the framework, so nothing raised it at any point.

The gap is now reported where operators actually read findings, as `oauth.redirect-uri-allowlist-missing`. It does NOT refuse: with no allowlist the guard cannot say a redirect_uri is wrong, only that it was given nothing to compare against, and refusing would make the primitive unusable before it is configured.

An EMPTY allowlist is a different thing and now behaves like one. `allowedRedirectUris: []` is a configuration that permits nothing — the shape you would use to deny callbacks until config loads — so every redirect_uri fails the exact-match check and is refused, rather than being read as an absent allowlist. A populated allowlist still refuses any URI outside it.

items.title: `b.base32.decode` accepted malformed padding
items.body:
RFC 4648 §6 fixes how many `=` a given symbol count takes. The decoder counted none of them, so `MZXW6YTBOI=====` and `MZXW6YTBOI=======` both decoded as readily as the correct `MZXW6YTBOI======`, and several spellings of one secret compared unequal while meaning the same bytes — the malleability this module already refuses for a final symbol's unused bits.

A wrong non-zero padding count is now refused with `base32/bad-padding`. Entirely unpadded input is still accepted, because `b.base32.encode(buf, { padding: false })` emits exactly that; `loose: true` continues to accept any padding, which is what hand-typed codes and TOTP secrets need.

items.title: Three documented examples produced a different answer than they printed
items.body:
`b.base32.encode(Buffer.from("foobar"))` was documented as `"MFRGGZDFMZTWQ===="`. That is the encoding of `"abcdefgh"`, with one padding character too many; `"foobar"` encodes to `"MZXW6YTBOI======"`. The decode example then round-tripped the same wrong string back to `"foobar"`, so the pair agreed with each other and with nothing else.

The `composeGates` example claimed a chain refuses a CSV containing a social-security number. It does not: the posture it sets governs redaction on serialize, which a gate validating incoming bytes never reaches. The example now shows a payload the chain actually acts on, and the disposition it actually returns.
